title: Bob Dylan and Protest Folk
subject: art
description: From Greenwich Village to the Nobel Prize, Bob Dylan turns folk song into political poetry, then into electric rock.

hero.hook: One guitar, one harmonica, and American song becomes literature.

blocks.text: **Bob Dylan**, born Robert Zimmerman in **1941** in Minnesota, is one of the most influential figures in 20th-century song. First a prophet of protest, then an electric poet, he refused to stay in a single box.
In **2016**, the Swedish Academy awarded him the **Nobel Prize in Literature**. For the first time, a rock songwriter was recognized as a major writer in the English language.

sections.title: Greenwich Village and the legacy of Woody Guthrie

blocks.text: In January **1961**, at 19, Zimmerman left the cold of the Midwest for **New York**. He had already chosen the name Bob Dylan. His idol was the folk singer **Woody Guthrie**, the voice of workers and of the oppressed, by then in the hospital. Dylan wanted to meet that American authenticity face to face.

He settled in **Greenwich Village**, the bohemian quarter of Manhattan. It was the heart of the [[folk revival]], the movement that dug up traditional songs and turned them into a tool of social criticism. Dylan worked the coffee houses, soaked up blues, country and gospel, and discovered poetry and the [[Beat Generation]].

blocks.caption: Greenwich Village in the 1960s: coffee houses, guitars and protest

blocks.text: Noticed for his phrasing and his raw harmonica, he signed with [[Columbia Records]] at the end of **1961**. The legend began.
Early on, Dylan made up his own biography. He claimed he had run away from a circus or traveled with carnivals, to build himself an outsider's aura.

sections.title: The protest song and the March on Washington

blocks.text: In **1963**, the album *The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan* changed everything. *Blowin' in the Wind* became an anthem. Dylan used [[Music as a political tool]]: simple melodies carrying messages about racism, war and nuclear fear.

In August **1963**, he sang at the **March on Washington** for civil rights, in front of **250,000** people, just before the speech by **Martin Luther King**. Yet he was already turning down the role of “spokesman for a generation”. His lyrics grew more surreal and more personal.

blocks.caption: August 1963: the March on Washington, a turning point for civil rights

blocks.text: That same year, television producers rejected him at an audition. They thought he sang too far off key.

In July **1965**, at the Newport Folk Festival, Dylan walked on stage with an electric [[Fender Stratocaster]]. Part of the purist audience booed him: electricity, they said, was a commercial betrayal. In fact, folk rock was being born.

blocks.caption: Newport 1965: Dylan plugs in, and an era turns

blocks.text: A founding trilogy followed: *Bringing It All Back Home*, *Highway 61 Revisited*, *Blonde on Blonde*. *Like a Rolling Stone* blew up the radio formats. Dylan was no longer only accusing society. He explored disillusion and the mind, with a verbal energy never heard before at the top of the charts.
The Newport Stratocaster was lost for 47 years, forgotten on a plane, then sold at auction for close to a million dollars in 2013.

sections.title: From the Never Ending Tour to the Nobel

blocks.text: After a motorcycle crash in **1966**, Dylan reinvented himself again and again: country, gospel, standards. His influence reached **John Lennon**, **Jimi Hendrix** and generations of songwriters. The **2016** Nobel settled the argument: song lyrics can be great literature.
